title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection
authors: Ghulam Mudassir, Hameed Ullah Khan, Ahmad Sami Al-Shamayleh, Muhammad Faizan Khan, Muhammad Muqtasid, Moamin Abughazala
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has several transformative effects on healthcare, like to facilitate clinicians in disease detection and to manage patient care with enhanced precision. Due to the increasing complexity of medical data and the growing volume of diagnostic images, the substantial computational power needed to process such information creates both opportunities and challenges. To accomplish this objective, numerous methodologies have been proposed to integrate AI into disease detection systems. All these methodologies consider different aspects of clinical diagnosis, considering key parameters such as the type of AI model employed, the nature of input data, and the population demographics being analysed. In this paper, we review different state-of-the-art techniques which have been proposed for various areas of disease detection, specifically focusing on bias identification and mitigation. The proposed solutions are distinguished based on the type of input data they utilize, the architecture of model, and type of bias (algorithmic bias, demographic bias, model bias, and deployment bias). The time frame chosen to filter out relevant studies is between 2015 and 2026. Eventually, we review 23 related articles out of 64,389 analyzed from seven different digital libraries. The obtained results guide us to reach a conclusion with respect to state-of-the-art selected studies. Furthermore, these results reveal significant research gaps that can assist researchers in addressing AI-related bias in medical diagnosis. By prioritizing explainability, data diversity, and fairness in algorithmic design, as well as equitable access for affected patient populations, they can utilize available healthcare resources more effectively.

infographic.key_insight: This review maps bias in AI disease detection and highlights data diversity, explainability, and fairness-aware design as priorities for more equitable systems.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Bias in diagnostic AI may contribute to unequal performance across patient populations, making fairness evaluation important before clinical deployment.
method: Reviewed disease-detection AI literature using a stated 2015–2026 study window.
Categorized approaches by input data, model architecture, and bias type.
Examined algorithmic, demographic, model, and deployment bias.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports reviewing 23 articles from 64,389 records across seven digital libraries, without quantitative estimates of bias reduction or diagnostic performance.
infographic.watch_item: The review identifies research priorities but does not establish that any mitigation strategy reliably improves fairness in clinical practice.
infographic.paper_title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection

title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
authors: Jiayan Yang, Ad Feelders, Arno Siebes
abstract: Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays. This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. Instead of relying on naive deterministic aggregation or fixed safety buffers, the framework explicitly models dynamic predictive uncertainty and evaluates extreme shortage exposure using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). These aggregated, risk-calibrated demand signals are then embedded into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy to generate delay-constrained staffing decisions. Evaluated on realistic trajectories from the MIMIC-IV database, the proposed framework demonstrates a favorable cost-shortage trade-off compared to deterministic and purely reactive baselines. Pareto frontier analysis illustrates how uncertainty-aware demand construction changes resource allocation under varying safety preferences, while stress testing confirms the framework's operational robustness even when subjected to systematic predictive bias in the form of calibration drift. By formalizing this translation layer, this work provides a principled, transparent pathway for safely integrating probabilistic AI outputs into high-stakes healthcare operational systems.

infographic.key_insight: An uncertainty-aware framework translates predicted patient deterioration risk into ICU staffing plans while accounting for hiring delays and extreme shortage risk.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support ICU workforce planning by balancing staffing costs against shortage exposure, but patient-care benefits remain unproven.
method: Model dynamic uncertainty in patient risk estimates without changing the predictive model.
Use Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) to assess extreme shortage exposure.
Feed risk-calibrated demand into hourly rolling-horizon scheduling with operational constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on realistic MIMIC-IV trajectories showed a favorable cost–shortage trade-off versus deterministic and reactive baselines, with stress tests assessing robustness to calibration drift.
infographic.watch_item: Real-world deployment needs prospective validation; the abstract reports no patient outcomes or numerical effect sizes.
infographic.paper_title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing

title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis
authors: Jian Yang, Peiling Liu, Songda Li, Yu Cao, Yuqing Feng, Lan Yu
abstract: Rare diseases (RDs) affect an estimated 300 million people globally, leaving patients to navigate a protracted diagnostic odyssey constrained by clinical scarcity and fragmented medical knowledge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively advanced RD diagnostics, from symbolic methods and deep learning to large language model (LLM)-based systems. However, each paradigm carries structural limitations: symbolic methods are bounded by knowledge completeness, neural models sacrifice interpretability, and LLM-based systems are vulnerable to evaluation biases like data leakage. In this study, we introduce FusionRare, a unified multiparadigm fusion framework integrating knowledge-driven symbolic reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, case-based patient retrieval, and LLM-based heuristic inference via statistical meta-aggregation and knowledge-enhanced agentic reflection. Evaluated on 2,528 strictly isolated clinical cases, FusionRare achieves state-of-the-art RD prioritization, attaining a macro-averaged Recall @1 of 51% for phenotype-only diagnosis and 79% for phenotype-genotype joint analysis. These results represent decisive advantages over the advanced agentic system DeepRare, frontier LLMs including GPT 5.5, and specialized tools like PhenoBrain and LIRICAL under stringent anti-leakage protocols. A randomized, crossover clinician-AI validation demonstrated that FusionRare elevates the true diagnostic rank in 45% of decisions, improves physician confidence in 62%, and reduces time to diagnosis by 21%. These findings indicate that reconciling these orthogonal AI paradigms significantly enhances diagnostic capabilities, bridging the gap between computational benchmarks and actionable clinical reliability. More broadly, this work provides a replicable framework for deploying trustworthy diagnostic AI across complex, high-stakes, and underserved medical domains.

infographic.key_insight: FusionRare combines complementary AI approaches and reports macro-averaged Recall@1 of 51% using phenotypes alone and 79% using phenotypes plus genotypes for rare-disease prioritization.
infographic.clinical_relevance: In a clinician-AI study, FusionRare improved the true diagnosis’s rank in 45% of decisions, increased physician confidence in 62%, and reduced reported time to diagnosis by 21%.
method: Combines symbolic reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, patient-case retrieval, and LLM inference.
Integrates outputs through statistical meta-aggregation and knowledge-enhanced agentic reflection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on 2,528 strictly isolated clinical cases under anti-leakage protocols, plus a randomized crossover clinician-AI validation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective real-world effectiveness; prioritization accuracy and clinician confidence do not by themselves confirm diagnostic safety.
infographic.paper_title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis

title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging
authors: Frank-Peter Schilling, Daniel Barco, Philipp Denzel, Marc Stadelmann
abstract: Generative deep learning methods such as Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks or Diffusion Models have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis. In particular, Diffusion Models have demonstrated superior image fidelity and sample diversity compared to other approaches on standard benchmarks, while also offering more flexible training dynamics as evidenced both in natural image domains and in medical applications. In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory, compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

infographic.key_insight: This review compares 3D diffusion models for medical imaging, highlighting their synthesis capabilities and the resource demands of volumetric data.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Potential applications include medical image reconstruction, data augmentation, domain transfer, inpainting, and artifact correction, rather than established clinical benefit.
method: Reviews 3D diffusion models for CT, MRI, and PET imaging.
Discusses conditioning on patient characteristics, reports, segmentation masks, or other images.
Compares current performance, limitations, and future research directions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a comparative overview but reports no dataset sizes, quantitative evaluation results, or clinical validation.
infographic.watch_item: Volumetric modeling requires substantial memory, compute, and training data, which may constrain implementation.
infographic.paper_title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging

title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
authors: Changshuo Liu, Jiaqi Zhu, Wenqiao Zhang, Xiaokui Xiao, Beng Chin Ooi
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.

infographic.key_insight: CODA combines patient-cohort patterns with individual deviations to support multimodal clinical reasoning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach aims to contextualize patient-specific information within similar patient groups for clinical question answering and report generation.
method: Uses reinforcement learning to discover patient cohorts.
Represents each patient's deviation from a cohort prototype as a structured drift signal.
Incorporates cohort and drift representations into a multimodal foundation model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability on real-world EHR benchmarks covering closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark results alone do not establish clinical safety or performance across new hospitals and patient populations.
infographic.paper_title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning

title: TIM: Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model for Longitudinal Radiology Report Generation
authors: Yiheng Dong, Yi Lin, Shilong Huang, Xiyan Yang, Xin Yang
abstract: Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) aims to translate medical images into diagnostic text, reducing radiologists' workload and standardizing clinical documentation. Nonetheless, existing approaches mainly focus on single-timepoint analysis and fail to capture temporal disease evolution across longitudinal examinations. While recent longitudinal RRG (LRRG) approaches incorporate historical data, they often combine images from different time points within a single representation space, leading to blurred semantics and inconsistent temporal reasoning. In this work, we propose a Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model (TIM), a two-stage framework that explicitly decouples spatial pathology from temporal progression and iteratively refines reports through mutual feedback. Stage I performs temporal-decoupled representation learning, separating temporal evolution patterns from disease-specific features and generating radiology reports for both prior and current studies. Stage II introduces a mutual report refinement mechanism that identifies diagnostic inconsistencies within prior reports and iteratively rectifies both prior and current reports through error-sensitive feedback. Experiments on the Longitudinal-MIMIC dataset demonstrate that TIM surpasses existing single-image and longitudinal baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art performance across both language and clinical metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/yihengd/TIM.

infographic.key_insight: TIM separates disease-specific image features from temporal changes, then iteratively refines prior and current reports to improve longitudinal radiology report generation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more consistent descriptions of disease evolution across serial imaging studies, though clinical benefit remains unestablished.
method: Separate spatial pathology features from temporal evolution patterns.
Generate initial reports for prior and current studies.
Use error-sensitive mutual feedback to iteratively refine both reports.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Longitudinal-MIMIC, TIM reportedly outperformed single-image and longitudinal baselines on language and clinical metrics; the abstract provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Refining prior reports could propagate errors across time points, warranting validation and clinician review before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: TIM: Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model for Longitudinal Radiology Report Generation

title: GraphBEAT: Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation Over Time for Early Risk Stratification of Gastrointestinal Cancers
authors: Leo Y. Li-Han, Chris Varghese, Elizabeth B. Habermann, Mark J. Truty, William R. G. Perry, Cornelius A. Thiels
abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) contain complementary diagnostic and laboratory information about patient health. However, irregularity, sparsity, heterogeneity, and incompleteness in documentation complicate EHR modeling. To address the problem, we introduce GraphBEAT (Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation over Time), a temporal graph representation learning framework that groups clinical events into time buckets and transforms observed features into patient-specific, temporally directed graphs to enable early risk stratification for gastrointestinal cancers. Each node in an EHR graph encodes feature identity, observed value, and temporal position of clinical events. A context-aware, time-decay message-passing mechanism models transitions between successive buckets, followed by multi-head attention pooling to generate patient-level representations. GraphBEAT was trained and evaluated on multi-site longitudinal diagnosis codes and laboratory tests to predict pancreatic, liver, and intestinal cancer at 12-, 24-, and 36-month diagnostic lead times. In all experimental setups, GraphBEAT consistently outperformed baseline graph neural networks (GraphSAGE, GAT, and GCN) and sequence modeling approaches (Transformer and long short-term memory [LSTM]). GraphBEAT also required over 250x fewer floating-point operations per patient and over 20x fewer parameters than the Transformer and LSTM baselines. These results support GraphBEAT as an accurate and computationally efficient approach for cancer risk stratification from sparse, heterogeneous longitudinal health records.

infographic.key_insight: GraphBEAT outperformed tested graph and sequence models for gastrointestinal cancer risk prediction while using substantially less computation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support earlier risk stratification for pancreatic, liver, and intestinal cancers using longitudinal diagnosis codes and laboratory results.
method: Groups clinical events into time buckets and builds patient-specific, temporally directed graphs.
Encodes event identity, observed value, and timing in graph nodes.
Combines context-aware, time-decay message passing with multi-head attention pooling.
infographic.evidence_signal: In multi-site EHR evaluations at 12-, 24-, and 36-month diagnostic lead times, GraphBEAT outperformed GraphSAGE, GAT, GCN, Transformer, and LSTM baselines, with over 250× fewer FLOPs per patient and over 20× fewer parameters than the sequence baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report cohort size, absolute predictive performance, or prospective validation, limiting assessment of clinical readiness.
infographic.paper_title: GraphBEAT: Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation Over Time for Early Risk Stratification of Gastrointestinal Cancers

title: DeliMF: Gated Cross-Attention Fusion of Structured Time Series and Clinical Text for Early Intensive Care Delirium Prediction
authors: Yibo Yang, Zerui Huang, Haomiao Yang, Zixia Wang
abstract: Delirium affects a large fraction of intensive care unit (ICU) patients and foreshadows longer stays, lasting cognitive decline, and higher mortality. Flagging the patients who will become delirious within the first day of admission would give clinicians a window to intervene. Yet state-of-the-art predictors rely only on the structured electronic health record (EHR) of vital signs, laboratory values, and medications, while overlooking the free-text clinical notes written in the same window, which carry information the numbers cannot encode. To this end, we present DeliMF, a multimodal framework that fuses the structured time series with clinical text. It encodes the structured signals with a temporal Transformer and the time-stamped radiology reports with a clinical text encoder, and fuses the two through a gated cross-attention module. The gate learns a per-patient weight on the text; when a patient has no note the gate closes and DeliMF reduces to its structured-only form, giving robustness to missing text by construction. On an incident-only MIMIC-IV cohort, DeliMF improves significantly over the baselines, particularly on patients who carry clinical text, while losing nothing on those without. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of multimodal fusion and gated cross-attention, and a case study further shows that fusing clinical text with the structured stream recovers delirium cases that the structured data alone misses. We hope DeliMF encourages early ICU prediction to make fuller use of the overlooked clinical text and contributes to the early identification and timely intervention of delirium.

infographic.key_insight: DeliMF combines structured ICU time series with clinical text to improve early delirium prediction, while reverting to structured-only prediction when text is unavailable.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Earlier identification of patients at risk of delirium could support timely clinical assessment, but clinical benefit has not been established.
method: Encode structured EHR time series with a temporal Transformer.
Encode time-stamped radiology reports with a clinical text encoder.
Fuse modalities through gated cross-attention with a patient-specific text weight.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an incident-only MIMIC-IV cohort, the abstract reports significant gains over baselines, especially for patients with text, with no reported performance loss for those without; ablations support the fusion design.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical performance estimates or external validation, leaving effect size and generalizability uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: DeliMF: Gated Cross-Attention Fusion of Structured Time Series and Clinical Text for Early Intensive Care Delirium Prediction

title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks
authors: Shenqi Zhou, Qiran Zou, Wenhao Zhao, Zhenyu Liao, Dianbo Liu
abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of developing machine learning (ML) models end to end. In medical practice, however, strong performance on the target metric does not fully characterize how good the models are in real-world use cases. For example, medical ML models should also provide well-calibrated risk estimates and remain robust across patient populations. Yet autonomous model development is typically guided by task objectives that emphasize simple predictive discrimination (e.g. AUROC). This raises a key question: are these objectives sufficient to guide agents toward models that meet the broader requirements of real-world medical use? In this study, we introduce Auto-MD-bench, a benchmark of 15 real-world medical tasks from 10 clinical datasets, spanning survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. We evaluate four agents: AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex, and Autoresearch. The strongest agents achieve competitive primary scores, yet their predicted risks are less calibrated than those of the simple baseline models, which could lead to severe medical accidents. Moreover, models with nearly identical primary scores can exhibit markedly different calibration, while performance varies substantially across population shifts. These findings show that primary task performance alone is insufficient to assess autonomous clinical modeling and multiple different metrics widely used in healthcare practice need to be taken into consideration.

infographic.key_insight: Strong primary predictive scores did not guarantee well-calibrated risk estimates or consistent performance across patient populations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating autonomous medical modeling requires calibration and robustness checks alongside primary predictive metrics.
method: Introduced Auto-MD-bench for survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction.
Evaluated AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex and Autoresearch against simple baseline models.
Assessed calibration and external performance across cohorts, hospitals and time periods.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 15 tasks from 10 clinical datasets, the strongest agents achieved competitive primary scores but produced less-calibrated risk estimates than simple baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark results do not establish clinical safety; calibration and population-shift performance need validation before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks

title: TRACE: Tracking Multimodal Clinical Trajectories for Inpatient Risk Prediction
authors: Minjun Kim, Jong Hak Moon
abstract: Accurate inpatient risk prediction requires modeling heterogeneous clinical evidence that accumulates irregularly over time. This challenge spans in-hospital mortality, prolonged length of stay, and readmission, each with task-specific observation windows. Existing multimodal approaches combine structured health record data, chest x-rays, and clinical text, but primarily focus on modality fusion or missing-modality compensation, with limited attention to temporal trajectories over an admission. We propose TRACE (TRAjectory modeling of multimodal Clinical Events), a daily-scale framework organizing clinical events into day-level trajectories, separating day-invariant global context from day-specific local events drawn from EHR data, chest x-rays, radiology reports, and discharge summaries. The trajectory is encoded using temporal attention, allowing unavailable modalities to emit no tokens. A phenotype-guided contrastive objective further organizes admissions under heterogeneous disease distributions. Across cohorts from MIMIC-IV, eICU, and MIMIC-III comprising nearly 180,000 total stays, we evaluate TRACE on mortality, length of stay, and readmission prediction. TRACE achieves the highest AUROC across all nine dataset-task settings and the highest ACC in eight, outperforming baselines. Ablation studies validate our attention masks and contrastive learning, while trajectory-level attribution localizes risk-associated hospital days and modalities.

infographic.key_insight: TRACE models day-by-day multimodal hospital trajectories and reports the highest AUROC across nine inpatient risk-prediction settings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support assessment of in-hospital mortality, prolonged length of stay, and readmission risk, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Separates day-invariant context from daily EHR, chest x-ray, radiology-report, and discharge-summary events.
Uses temporal attention to encode trajectories, with unavailable modalities emitting no tokens.
Applies phenotype-guided contrastive learning and attributes predictions to hospital days and modalities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across nearly 180,000 stays from MIMIC-IV, eICU, and MIMIC-III, TRACE achieved the highest AUROC in all nine dataset-task settings and highest accuracy in eight.
infographic.watch_item: Because discharge summaries are included, task-specific time cutoffs require careful verification to prevent use of information unavailable at prediction time.
infographic.paper_title: TRACE: Tracking Multimodal Clinical Trajectories for Inpatient Risk Prediction

title: Localization Gains from Explanation Regularization Should Not Be Interpreted as Faithfulness Gains.
authors: Amrin Akter, Mauro Dalla Mura, Diana Mateus, Dawood Al Chanti
abstract: Training-time explanation regularization is often evaluated by whether saliency maps become more concentrated within annotated regions. We argue that this criterion alone is insufficient: transformation consistency, lesion localization, and faithfulness to the classifier are distinct properties and should be evaluated separately, particularly in medical imaging. We examine this distinction through a case study of Contrastive Grad-CAM Consistency (CGC) in three-class brain tumor MRI classification. Using a single-channel ResNet-50 with five-fold patient-grouped cross-validation, we compare a cross-entropy baseline with CGC. CGC changes overall Pointing Game (PG) from $27.24\%$ to $36.02\%$ and Relevance Mass Accuracy (RMA) from $11.17\%$ to $18.01\%$, while classification accuracy changes from $93.63\%$ to $94.87\%$. Perturbation-based faithfulness metrics show inconsistent changes: Insertion Area Under the Curve (IAUC) changes from $0.73$ to $0.78$, whereas Deletion Area Under the Curve (DAUC) favors the baseline ($0.36$ versus $0.41$; lower is better), and overall Iterative Removal Of Features (IROF) is $0.57$ for both models. These results support our position that improved spatial agreement with pathology should not be interpreted as a general improvement in explanation faithfulness. We therefore recommend property-specific evaluation in which the property targeted by the explanation objective, spatial agreement with reference regions, and model reliance are measured and reported separately.

infographic.key_insight: More lesion-focused saliency maps do not necessarily explain a classifier’s decisions more faithfully.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For medical imaging AI, better overlap with pathology should not be treated as proof that an explanation reliably reflects model reliance.
method: Compared cross-entropy training with Contrastive Grad-CAM Consistency in three-class brain tumor MRI classification.
Used a single-channel ResNet-50 with five-fold patient-grouped cross-validation.
Evaluated classification accuracy, lesion localization, and perturbation-based faithfulness separately.
infographic.evidence_signal: CGC improved Pointing Game from 27.24% to 36.02% and accuracy from 93.63% to 94.87%, but faithfulness was mixed: insertion improved, deletion worsened, and IROF was unchanged.
infographic.watch_item: This single case study does not establish generalizability across datasets, architectures, or explanation-regularization methods.
infographic.paper_title: Localization Gains from Explanation Regularization Should Not Be Interpreted as Faithfulness Gains.

title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
authors: Savan Doshi
abstract: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. We introduce a risk-sensitive evaluation framework that scores responses by the presence and severity of six categories of risk-bearing language (treatment directives, contraindications, dosage expressions, urgency-triage cues, high-alert medication mentions, and overconfident assertions), anchored on published clinical harm taxonomies. Severity is classified by a three-judge LLM ensemble. We apply this framework to six 7-9B instruction-tuned models, three general (Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3.1-8B) and three medically adapted (BioMistral-7B, OpenBioLLM-Llama3-8B, Med42-Llama3-8B), on 200 real patient questions from the K-QA benchmark. Two findings emerge. First, ensemble risk-bearing language is statistically independent of factual hallucination rate (pooled Spearman $ρ= -0.065$, $n = 300$, 95% CI $[-0.18, +0.05]$; distance correlation $= 0.10$, independence test $p = 0.24$). Second, medical fine-tuning does not reduce aggregate risk but reshapes it: continued-pretraining adaptations (BioMistral, OpenBioLLM) consistently suppress high-alert medication mentions while amplifying overconfident assertions, whereas clinical instruction-tuning (Med42) suppresses dosing only, without amplifying overconfidence. Per-category Krippendorff $α$ is fair to good for the four linguistically anchored categories (0.53-0.71) and low for the two clinical-judgment-dependent categories (0.19, 0.31), indicating where automatic safety evaluation is and is not yet reliable. We release the rubric, judge prompts, and evaluation code.

infographic.key_insight: Medical adaptation reshaped rather than reduced aggregate risk-bearing language, which was not significantly associated with factual hallucination rates.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Patient-facing medical AI evaluation should assess potentially harmful language alongside factual accuracy.
method: Evaluated six general and medically adapted instruction-tuned models on 200 real patient questions from K-QA.
Scored six categories of risk-bearing language using a clinical-harm-informed rubric.
Used a three-judge LLM ensemble to classify severity and compared adaptation-specific risk patterns.
infographic.evidence_signal: Risk-bearing language and hallucination rates showed little association (pooled Spearman ρ = −0.065; n = 300; 95% CI −0.18 to 0.05), while category-level judge agreement varied substantially (Krippendorff α = 0.19–0.71).
infographic.watch_item: Low judge agreement in clinical-judgment-dependent categories limits automated evaluation reliability; these language-based scores do not establish actual patient harm.
infographic.paper_title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework

title: HGASurv: Hierarchical Granularity-Aware Integration for Multimodal Survival Prediction
authors: Peike Yu, Wuchao Liu, Jihong Guan, Shuigeng Zhou
abstract: Objective: Multimodal survival prediction jointly analyzes histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), genomic profiles, and clinical variables to stratify patients by risk. However, existing approaches often inadequately account for granularity differences across modalities, particularly in spatial organization and feature dimensionality. To address these challenges, we propose HGASurv, which introduces a hierarchical WSI encoding module and a clinical-guided graph propagation module for granularity-aware multimodal integration. Methods: The hierarchical WSI encoding module maps WSI patch features onto a spatial grid using their original coordinates and applies parallel convolutions to construct representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Genomic signature embeddings then query these scale-specific WSI representations through cross-modal co-attention, producing signature-conditioned morphological features. The clinical-guided graph propagation module uses clinical variables to define patient-similarity edges and propagates fused image-genomic node embeddings with graph attention, integrating clinical information through topology rather than feature concatenation. Results: Across three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv achieved the strongest overall C-index performance, with ablation studies supporting the complementary contributions of the hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation modules. Conclusion and Significance: By introducing hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation, HGASurv unifies multi-scale pathology representation with topology-based clinical integration in a hierarchical granularity-aware framework. This design shows that matching representation and integration mechanisms to modality-specific granularity improves multimodal survival prediction.

infographic.key_insight: HGASurv combines multi-scale pathology features, genomic signatures, and clinical similarity to improve multimodal survival prediction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support cancer risk stratification, but the abstract does not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Encode whole-slide image patches at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales using spatial coordinates.
Use genomic signatures to query multi-scale image features through cross-modal co-attention.
Propagate fused image–genomic features across a patient graph defined by clinical similarity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv reported the strongest overall C-index performance among evaluated methods, with ablations supporting both proposed modules.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no external validation, leaving generalizability beyond the evaluated TCGA cohorts uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: HGASurv: Hierarchical Granularity-Aware Integration for Multimodal Survival Prediction

title: When to Stop Asking: Factor Coverage Bias and LLM Determinability Judgments with Underspecified Information in Medicine
authors: Yusuke Watanabe, Yohei Kobashi, Taisei Tosaki, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yasushi Okuno
abstract: Clinical decision-making often begins with underspecified information and requires not only gathering missing information but also knowing when to stop. This calls for judging determinability (whether the available information is sufficient for a decision) by considering whether missing information could change the conclusion, not simply the amount of available decision-relevant information. Reliance on this amount as a cue for determinability, which we term \textit{factor coverage bias}, could undermine the trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs) through premature conclusions or excessive information gathering, such as unnecessary invasive tests. Yet whether LLMs exhibit this bias remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we construct a controlled pairwise benchmark in which LLMs identify the determinable case within each determinable--undeterminable pair. We add a decision-relevant factor to either side while keeping each case's determinability unchanged, and similarly add irrelevant text to distinguish this bias from context-length effects. Adding a relevant factor made LLMs more likely to select the augmented case as determinable even when it remained undeterminable, an effect that persisted with increased reasoning effort, while adding irrelevant text made them less likely to select the augmented case, an effect that reasoning substantially reduced. These findings identify factor coverage bias as a failure mode distinct from context-length effects and a potential risk to LLM trustworthiness. Our work provides an evaluation framework for LLM trustworthiness under underspecification.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs can mistake more decision-relevant information for sufficient information, even when missing details could still change the conclusion—a failure termed factor coverage bias.
infographic.clinical_relevance: In clinical decision support, this bias could contribute to premature conclusions or unnecessary information gathering, including potentially invasive tests.
method: Constructed paired cases with one determinable and one undeterminable decision.
Added a relevant factor to either case without changing its determinability.
Compared relevant-factor additions with irrelevant text additions and tested increased reasoning effort.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the controlled benchmark, relevant-factor additions increased selection of the augmented case as determinable despite increased reasoning effort, while irrelevant text reduced selection—an effect substantially reduced by reasoning.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports controlled benchmark findings, not real-world clinical outcomes, so clinical impact remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: When to Stop Asking: Factor Coverage Bias and LLM Determinability Judgments with Underspecified Information in Medicine

title: Trust the Edge, Doubt the Arrow: Auditing Validation Signals for Text-Mined Clinical Causal Knowledge Graphs
authors: Su Lan, Shicheng Zhou, Yiqi Wang, Yanming Zhu, Xuefei Yin, Alan Wee-Chung Liew
abstract: Clinical causal retrieval-augmented generation systems increasingly use knowledge graphs (KGs) mined from notes, yet extracted assertions remain candidates that require audit for patient-level EHR support and direction. We construct a directed candidate graph from 328,839 MIMIC-IV discharge summaries using LLM extraction and UMLS normalization, and evaluate three signals against SemMedDB: within-admission co-occurrence lift, cross-admission diagnosis-coding temporal precedence, and literature corroboration. Lift filters unsupported co-mentions and provides useful EHR support, but not causal proof. Coding order is a weak direction signal: among the 686 candidates where it commits, it reaches 54.2% agreement with SemMedDB, below the extractor's 69.4% on the same subset. Literature corroboration supplies independent direction evidence but covers only 30.4% of candidate relations. A MIMIC-III replication yields the same pattern: extractor direction remains stable (70.5%), whereas coding-order direction is near chance (50.9%). Thus, text-mined clinical causal candidate KGs are best treated as EHR-supported but direction-uncertain. In a leakage-controlled causal QA benchmark, lift-only retrieval achieves 35.7% accuracy; conservative causal demotion achieves 37.2% while reducing evidence-unsupported answers from 17.3% to 6.1% at fixed retrieval recall. We release code, aggregate summaries, and scripts to regenerate restricted outputs.

infographic.key_insight: Text-mined clinical knowledge graphs can identify EHR-supported relationships, but causal direction remains uncertain and should not be inferred from diagnosis-coding order alone.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Conservatively downgrading uncertain causal claims may help clinical AI systems produce fewer evidence-unsupported answers without sacrificing retrieval recall.
method: Extracted directed candidate relations from 328,839 MIMIC-IV discharge summaries using an LLM and UMLS normalization.
Evaluated co-occurrence lift, diagnosis-coding temporal precedence, and literature corroboration against SemMedDB, with MIMIC-III replication.
Compared lift-only retrieval with conservative causal demotion in a leakage-controlled causal QA benchmark.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 686 candidates with a coding-order direction, agreement with SemMedDB was 54.2% versus 69.4% for extraction; causal demotion reduced evidence-unsupported QA answers from 17.3% to 6.1% while accuracy rose from 35.7% to 37.2%.
infographic.watch_item: Co-occurrence support is not causal proof, and literature corroboration covered only 30.4% of candidate relations.
infographic.paper_title: Trust the Edge, Doubt the Arrow: Auditing Validation Signals for Text-Mined Clinical Causal Knowledge Graphs

title: Doubly Robust Learning of Heterogeneous Survival Treatment Effects under Time-Varying Treatments
authors: Tomàs Garriga, Munib Mesinovic, Luke De Bretton-Gordon, Gerard Sanz, Axel Brando, Tingting Zhu
abstract: Estimating heterogeneous survival treatment effects (HSTEs) from time-to-event data under time-varying treatments is important in fields such as medicine (e.g., to decide which sequence of treatments is better in terms of survival probability). However, this task is challenging because treatment decisions, patient characteristics, and censoring probability often evolve together, requiring sequential adjustment for both treatments and censoring. Existing survival learners mostly consider a single baseline treatment assignment, while longitudinal treatment-effect learners typically assume uncensored outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a novel doubly robust learner for heterogeneous survival treatment effects under time-varying treatments and history-dependent censoring. Our framework separates the intervention window from the survival horizon, with treatment prescribed for a finite period, after which care follows its natural course. We further establish the favorable theoretical properties of Neyman-orthogonality, rate double robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. The framework accommodates flexible machine learning models for nuisance estimation and treatment-effect regression. We evaluate our learners through several numerical experiments, demonstrating their effectiveness.

infographic.key_insight: A doubly robust learning framework estimates how survival effects of time-varying treatment strategies differ across individuals while accounting for history-dependent censoring.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support research comparing finite treatment sequences by their longer-term survival effects, but it does not establish clinical benefit.
method: Separates the treatment intervention window from the survival horizon, allowing subsequent care to follow its natural course.
Sequentially adjusts for evolving treatment decisions and censoring using flexible machine learning.
Establishes Neyman orthogonality, rate double robustness, and quasi-oracle efficiency.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports several numerical experiments demonstrating effectiveness, without specifying datasets or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Real-world clinical validation is not described in the abstract, and doubly robust estimation does not eliminate reliance on causal assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: Doubly Robust Learning of Heterogeneous Survival Treatment Effects under Time-Varying Treatments

title: Morpheus: a fully local, defense-in-depth de-identification engine for Greek clinical text - a benchmark evaluation
authors: Filippos-Paschalis Rorris, Nikoleta Stanitsa, Tatiana Rorri, Foteini Rorri, Constantine N. Antonopoulos
abstract: Background and Objective: Clinical free text cannot leave the hospital without de-identification, yet no de-identification system or benchmark exists for Greek clinical text. We evaluated Morpheus, a fully local de-identification pipeline for Greek clinical documents, on 500 synthetic discharge summaries. Methods: The notes (300 cardiac surgery, 100 cardiology, 100 nephrology) were generated by a frontier large language model (Gemini 3.1 Pro) constrained to authentic Greek hospital document layouts. Notes were pre-annotated at generation; two clinicians then independently reviewed and corrected every note, blinded to each other, with disagreements arbitrated. Primary outcomes were recall over must-redact identifiers and over-redaction of clinical content, measured over must-survive probes. Secondary outcomes: residual leaks flagged by an independent egress-review layer, processing time and reproducibility. Results: Inter-annotator agreement was F1 = 0.998. The de-identification rate was 96.59% (7,666/7,937 identifier instances; 95% CI 96.16-96.96): 98.49% for direct and 93.42% for quasi-identifiers. No patient's own complete identifier survived in any note; of 271 residual instances, 199 (73.4%) concerned institutional identity, chiefly the hospital letterhead. The over-redaction rate was 2.82% (190/6,747 probes; 95% CI 2.45-3.24). The egress guard flagged 2 of 271 residuals, both complete telephone numbers. Two independent runs gave identical verdicts. Conclusions: A fully local, deterministic pipeline removed 98.5% of direct patient identifiers from Greek clinical text while altering under 3% of protected clinical content; most residuals concerned the institution, not the patient. To our knowledge this is the first benchmark evaluation of clinical-text de-identification for Greek and the first quantified evaluation of an independent egress-guard layer.

infographic.key_insight: Morpheus, a fully local Greek clinical-text de-identification pipeline, removed 96.59% of annotated identifiers while over-redacting 2.82% of protected clinical-content probes.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Local processing could support privacy-preserving reuse of Greek clinical notes without sending identifiable text outside hospital infrastructure.
method: Evaluated 500 LLM-generated Greek discharge summaries across cardiac surgery, cardiology and nephrology.
Two clinicians independently reviewed annotations, with disagreements arbitrated.
Measured identifier removal, clinical-content over-redaction, residual-leak detection and reproducibility.
infographic.evidence_signal: On synthetic notes, Morpheus removed 7,666 of 7,937 identifiers (95% CI 96.16–96.96%); two independent runs produced identical verdicts.
infographic.watch_item: Real-world validation remains needed: 271 identifier instances survived, mostly institutional identifiers, and the independent egress guard flagged only 2.
infographic.paper_title: Morpheus: a fully local, defense-in-depth de-identification engine for Greek clinical text - a benchmark evaluation

title: PFedQFT: Personalized Federated Quantum-Inspired Fine-Tuning for Medical Large Language Models
authors: Qihan Huang, Lingxia Zhang, Guye Zhang, Zizhu Wang, Xiaowei Mao
abstract: Medical data remain fragmented across institutional silos because of privacy, governance, and ownership constraints. Federated learning enables medical institutions to adapt large language models (LLMs) collaboratively without transferring raw records. However, independently parameterized low-rank adapters incur repeated parameter and communication costs across Transformer projections, while uniform aggregation may limit adaptation to heterogeneous institutional data. We propose PFedQFT, a quantum-inspired framework for personalized federated fine-tuning with a compact shared adapter. Specifically, PFedQFT constructs reusable orthonormal adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators using a truncated matrix-exponential approximation followed by QR orthonormalization. Compatible projections reuse these bases, while a globally shared full core preserves the flexibility of each projection. Each client further maintains a lightweight private residual operator, whose directions are learned globally and whose coefficients remain local. Experiments on seven public medical tasks and multiple LLM backbones show substantial reductions in trainable parameters and per-round adapter upload volume, with competitive predictive performance on most tasks.

infographic.key_insight: PFedQFT combines reusable compact adapters with local personalization to reduce federated fine-tuning overhead while maintaining competitive performance on most evaluated medical tasks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help institutions collaboratively adapt medical LLMs without transferring raw records while accommodating differences in local data.
method: Constructs reusable orthonormal adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators using an approximate matrix exponential and QR orthonormalization.
Shares bases across compatible Transformer projections and uses a globally shared full core.
Adds lightweight private residual operators with globally learned directions and locally retained coefficients.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on seven public medical tasks and multiple LLM backbones showed substantial reductions in trainable parameters and per-round adapter uploads, with competitive predictive performance on most tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Public-task results do not establish clinical readiness, and keeping raw records local does not by itself guarantee privacy.
infographic.paper_title: PFedQFT: Personalized Federated Quantum-Inspired Fine-Tuning for Medical Large Language Models

title: CoRe-WM: Conditioned Response-State World Modeling for Longitudinal Treatment-Response Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI
authors: Lin Zhao, Bowen Chen, Qiaohui Gao, Shaowen Wan, Xiang Li, Wei Liu
abstract: Pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a key prognostic indicator in aggressive breast cancer, yet existing prediction approaches either rely on pretreatment imaging alone, missing the patient's evolving response, or optimize multi-visit classifiers under direct outcome supervision, coupling representation learning with the clinical endpoint. We formulate longitudinal pCR prediction as a world-modeling problem and propose Conditioned Response-state World Modeling (CoRe-WM), which learns a latent state-transition model that predicts the next imaging state from the observed sequence. The transition function is conditioned on patient clinical profile and assigned therapy through additive shift and feature-wise modulation, enabling patient- and treatment-specific dynamics. A Factorized Response State pathway further decouples treatment-response dynamics from imaging appearance by encoding the structural prior that response manifests primarily in lesion morphology. After pretraining, all parameters are frozen and a linear readout predicts pCR at each clinical decision point. We evaluate CoRe-WM on I-SPY2 under five-fold cross-validation and assess cross-cohort transfer on I-SPY1. CoRe-WM achieves the highest discrimination among all evaluated methods at every prospective decision point, and demonstrates robust cross-cohort transfer. Ablation studies identify patient-profile conditioning and the factorized response pathway as the principal contributors. These results establish world-model-based representation learning as a promising framework for outcome prediction in oncology and beyond.

infographic.key_insight: CoRe-WM learns how breast MRI states evolve during treatment, then uses frozen representations to predict pathologic complete response (pCR).
infographic.clinical_relevance: Tracking evolving imaging response could improve pCR risk estimates during neoadjuvant chemotherapy, though clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Predicts the next latent imaging state from longitudinal DCE-MRI.
Conditions state transitions on patient clinical profiles and assigned therapy.
Separates morphology-focused response dynamics from imaging appearance, then predicts pCR with a linear readout.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports the highest discrimination among evaluated methods at every assessed decision point in five-fold I-SPY2 cross-validation, plus robust transfer to I-SPY1, without numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective validation is needed to establish whether predictions improve treatment decisions or patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: CoRe-WM: Conditioned Response-State World Modeling for Longitudinal Treatment-Response Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI

title: ClinSDT: LLM-Encoded Clinical Semantic Guidance for Sepsis Treatment via Decision Transformer
authors: Yanyan Wu, Guanyu Zhu, Changbin Zhao, Jin Zhang, Dexu Yu, Tianmin Sun
abstract: Offline sepsis treatment aims to learn treatment policies from retrospective ICU trajectories. Decision Transformer-based methods provide a natural sequence modeling framework for this task, but they mainly rely on raw physiological states and historical clinician actions. Such raw trajectory tokens may not explicitly capture clinical semantics that clinicians use in practice, such as patient severity, recent treatment response, and current risk priorities. To address this limitation, we propose ClinSDT, an LLM-assisted Decision Transformer framework for offline sepsis treatment. ClinSDT uses a frozen LLM as a semantic bridge rather than a treatment decision maker. It constructs three clinical semantic views from ICU trajectories, namely Profile, Context, and Advisory, and inserts their encoded representations as independent tokens into a Decision Transformer policy. To support policy refinement and rollout, ClinSDT further trains a Treatment-Response Forecaster to estimate the next physiological state, SAPS-II change, and predictive uncertainty from state-action inputs. In the second training stage, the forecaster screens local counterfactual treatment candidates, and only low-uncertainty candidates with lower predicted SAPS-II increase are distilled into the policy after semantic regeneration. During inference, ClinSDT performs closed-loop treatment rollout by refreshing semantic inputs from the currently available patient state. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that ClinSDT achieves consistent relative improvements over representative imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning, and Decision Transformer baselines under the same rollout protocol. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KAG778/ClinSDT.

infographic.key_insight: ClinSDT augments a Decision Transformer with LLM-encoded clinical semantics to learn sepsis treatment policies from retrospective ICU trajectories.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach aims to make learned treatment policies more sensitive to patient severity, recent treatment response, and current risk priorities.
method: A frozen LLM encodes Profile, Context, and Advisory views as separate policy tokens rather than directly choosing treatments.
A Treatment-Response Forecaster screens local treatment alternatives for low predictive uncertainty and lower predicted SAPS-II increase before policy refinement.
Closed-loop rollout refreshes semantic inputs using the currently available patient state.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV report consistent relative improvements over imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning, and Decision Transformer baselines under the same rollout protocol.
infographic.watch_item: Retrospective rollout improvements do not establish clinical safety or patient benefit; prospective validation is needed before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: ClinSDT: LLM-Encoded Clinical Semantic Guidance for Sepsis Treatment via Decision Transformer
